titre: Patient H.M. and the Two Memories
accroche: In 1953, an operation for epilepsy takes away his ability to form new memories, without touching his memory for movements.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1953, the surgeon William Beecher Scoville removes a large part of the medial temporal lobes of a twenty-seven-year-old man, hoping to relieve severe, uncontrollable epilepsy. The operation includes most of the hippocampus, on both sides of the brain. The epilepsy improves. But the patient, known for fifty-five years only by the initials H.M., will never again form a new conscious memory.

## A Case That Reshuffles the Deck

Scoville teams up with the neuropsychologist Brenda Milner to document what has just happened. Their 1957 article, which studies H.M. alongside eight other patients, describes an almost total anterograde amnesia: H.M. can hold a conversation, but forgets his interlocutor as soon as that person leaves the room. He rereads the same magazine without ever remembering having read it already.

Milner gives him a task that seems innocuous, which she publishes in 1962: tracing the outline of a double-outlined star while seeing his hand and the drawing only as reflected in a mirror, a difficult exercise for anyone. Over about ten trials, H.M. acquires this skill and keeps it over several days, his performance improving like that of any subject who practices. Yet at each new session, he does not remember having already done the exercise.

The contrast is the discovery: an intact memory for movements coexists with a total inability to consciously recall a lived event. This dissociation founded the distinction, now central in neuroscience, between declarative memory, facts and events, and procedural memory, know-how. Two systems, two distinct brain circuits, where before people spoke only of “one” memory.

## A File Revised Forty Years Later

The researcher Suzanne Corkin studies H.M. from 1962 until his death in 2008, forty-six years of follow-up of the same patient, a case without equivalent in neuroscience. His real name, Henry Molaison, is revealed only after his death.

In 1997, an MRI commissioned by Corkin and her colleagues corrects even the memory of the operation: Scoville believed he had removed nearly the entire hippocampus. The imaging shows that about two of the normal four centimeters of the hippocampus had in fact been spared, a detail that, decades later, fed a new generation of work on what this remaining fragment could still, or could not, accomplish.

The H.M. case thus did not merely reveal the existence of two memories. It is a reminder that an established fact can be revised, not by a new theory, but by a measuring instrument that did not yet exist.

repere.texte: The 1997 MRI showed that about two of the normal four centimeters of H.M.'s hippocampus had in fact been spared by the 1953 operation, contrary to what had been believed for forty years.
repere.source: Corkin, S., Amaral, D.G., González, R.G., Johnson, K.A., Hyman, B.T., Journal of Neuroscience, 1997

carte.punch: H.M. relearned the same drawing several days in a row, never remembering the day before.
carte.idee: In 1953, an operation for epilepsy removes a large part of Henry Molaison's hippocampus. He becomes unable to form new memories, but can still learn a movement without remembering having learned it, proof that there are several distinct memories.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: On Suzanne Corkin's decades of follow-up and her book Permanent Present Tense.

quiz.question: Why did the mirror-drawing task given to Henry Molaison leave its mark on the neuroscience of memory?
choix: It showed that he could remember faces but not words
It showed that he improved at the movement without remembering having done it, revealing two distinct memories
It proved that his hippocampus had partly regenerated after the operation
It showed that he retained verbal instructions but not movements
quiz.explication: His performance improved from trial to trial, procedural memory, tied to movement, remained intact, while he kept no conscious memory of having already done the exercise. This contrast was one of the first proofs that declarative memory and procedural memory rest on distinct brain circuits.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the surgeon William Beecher Scoville operate on H.M. in 1953?
choix: To remove a tumor detected in the temporal lobes
To experimentally test the effects of removing the hippocampus
To treat memory problems already present before the operation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Scoville removes a large part of H.M.'s medial temporal lobes hoping to relieve severe, uncontrollable epilepsy. The epilepsy does improve, but at the price of an almost total anterograde amnesia, an effect that was not sought.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the MRI commissioned by Suzanne Corkin in 1997 reveal?
choix: That H.M.'s hippocampus had begun to regenerate since 1953
That about two of the normal four centimeters of the hippocampus had in fact been spared
That the 1953 operation had affected a different region of the brain than the one planned
That H.M. had a second lesion, separate from the 1953 one
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Scoville believed he had removed nearly the entire hippocampus. The 1997 MRI shows that about two of the normal four centimeters had in fact been spared, a detail that fed new work on what this remaining fragment could still accomplish.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When is H.M.'s real name, Henry Molaison, revealed to the public?
choix: As soon as Scoville and Milner's article is published in 1957
In 1962, when Brenda Milner gives him the mirror-drawing task
In 1997, at the time of the MRI commissioned by Suzanne Corkin
quiz_supplementaire.explication: H.M. was known only by his initials for fifty-five years. His real name, Henry Molaison, was revealed only after his death in 2008, despite the decades of follow-up carried out in the meantime by Suzanne Corkin from 1962.
